name: Google Reader
epitaph: It read the world, so you didn't have to.
eulogy: Google Reader arrived in 2005 as a quiet miracle: one place for every blog, every news site, every RSS feed the internet could offer. Millions woke up to it like a morning newspaper. Engineers loved it. Journalists depended on it. Bloggers published for it. Then, on July 1, 2013, Google decided social sharing had already won and pulled the plug. The day of closure, the internet held a small funeral. Flowers were left in spreadsheets. Some users have never quite forgiven them. Little is left of it, but the grief was real.
survived_by: Feedly, Inoreader, and a generation of users who never stopped wanting it back.

name: GeoCities
epitaph: Every homepage was a masterpiece, in its own way.
eulogy: GeoCities was the universe's first attempt at giving everyone a corner of the internet to call their own. With blink tags, tiled backgrounds, animated GIFs of dancing hamsters, and MIDI files that started playing the moment you arrived, it was chaos — magnificent chaos. Yahoo acquired it in 1999 for $3.57 billion and spent a decade quietly suffocating it. On October 26, 2009, GeoCities and its 38 million pages vanished. Archive Team raced against the clock to save what they could. A whole aesthetic era died that day.
survived_by: Neocities, and every modern portfolio site that secretly wishes it could use a scrolling marquee.

name: Vine
epitaph: Six seconds. That's all it needed.
eulogy: Vine proved that creativity doesn't need time — it needs constraints. In six looping seconds, comedians built careers, memes were born, and an entire generation learned the grammar of short video. Twitter bought it before it launched, then ignored it while Instagram added 15-second video. On October 28, 2016, Twitter announced the shutdown. The creators it had launched — Shawn Mendes, Logan Paul, Zach King — moved on. The loops stopped looping. But every short-form video platform today is just Vine in a different outfit.
survived_by: TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts — the entire short-video internet.

name: Grooveshark
epitaph: It let you hear anything. That was the problem.
eulogy: Grooveshark was built in a dorm room in 2007 on a beautiful, reckless premise: let anyone upload any song and play it for free. The interface was clean, the library was staggering, and the legality was questionable. Major labels sued. Grooveshark fought. Executives wrote internal emails that became evidence in court. By 2015 the lawsuits won. The site went dark with a remarkably dignified apology homepage. It was a lesson in building something wonderful on a foundation that other people owned.
cause_label: Shut down following copyright lawsuit settlement
survived_by: Spotify, Apple Music, and a generation of music fans who still remember the interface.

name: Adobe Flash Player
epitaph: You needed to update it. Every. Single. Day.
eulogy: Flash was the engine of the early web's creativity: animations, games, entire interactive worlds that had no right to exist in a browser. Newgrounds. Homestar Runner. Online games that kids played secretly in school labs. Then Steve Jobs wrote a letter in 2010 explaining why the iPhone would never support it. The world nodded. Adobe set a death date. On December 31, 2020, Adobe pulled the plug and started actively blocking Flash content from running. An entire creative era became inaccessible overnight. Ruffle and archive projects have since tried to excavate it.
survived_by: HTML5 Canvas, WebGL, Unity WebGL — and the Ruffle emulator trying to save what remains.

name: StumbleUpon
epitaph: Serendipity, served one click at a time.
eulogy: StumbleUpon launched in 2002 as a way to discover the web by chance. Users clicked a button and the site used community votes to surface surprising pages. It grew into a cultural bookmarking staple with millions of daily stumbles. The design was playful, the discovery felt magical. In 2013 eBay acquired it and integrations faded. The service officially shut down on March 30, 2018, redirecting users to Mix. An entire generation of accidental browsing stopped.
cause_label: Shut down by owner following acquisition
survived_by: Mix, Pocket, and the memory of accidental finds.

name: Yahoo Answers
epitaph: How is babby formed? We may never know.
eulogy: Yahoo Answers was the world's largest repository of questions that should never have been asked, answered by people who probably shouldn't have answered them. And yet, among the chaos, there was real human knowledge: a diabetic patient asking about insulin, a teenager seeking help they couldn't ask their parents, a mechanic quietly solving a stranger's car problem at midnight. It was the internet's id. Yahoo shut it down on May 4, 2021, and the Archive Team saved what they could. The Library of Congress was not consulted.
survived_by: Reddit, Quora, and the continued failure to answer how babby is formed.

name: Picnik
epitaph: It made photo editing friendly, before the clouds took it.
eulogy: Picnik was the photo editor that lived in your browser before that was remarkable. No download. No Photoshop license. Just drag, drop, and charm — rounded corners, speech bubbles, vintage filters, all in a delightful Flash interface that felt like a toy and worked like a tool. Google acquired it in 2010 for an undisclosed sum and quietly folded it into Google+. In April 2012, Picnik closed — sacrificed on the altar of a social network nobody wanted. The goodbye page was one of the most cheerful shutdown notices ever written.
cause_label: Acquired by Google and shut down to absorb into Google+
survived_by: Canva, PicsArt, and Photopea — and Google+, which also died.

name: AltaVista
epitaph: The search engine that mapped the wild early web.
eulogy: AltaVista was born in DEC's Western Research Laboratory in 1995 and immediately set the standard for web search, crawling tens of millions of pages with unmatched speed. In the 1990s, it was the portal through which millions explored cyberspace. Then corporate acquisitions transferred it between Compaq, CMGI, Overture, and finally Yahoo in 2003. As Google perfected clean algorithmic relevance, AltaVista became a neglected Yahoo subsidiary. On July 8, 2013, Yahoo pulled the plug and redirected the domain to Yahoo Search. A titan of the early internet quietly vanished into the corporate background.
cause_label: Outcompeted by Google and shut down by Yahoo
survived_by: Google, Yahoo Search, and everyone who remembers when Babelfish was the only translator online.

name: ICQ
eulogy: ICQ — I Seek You — was the first messenger the internet ever loved. The 'uh oh' notification sound was the sound of connection in 1996, when the world was just learning to talk in real time. AOL acquired it in 1998. MSN Messenger arrived and took users. Then WhatsApp took them all. ICQ changed hands to a Russian company, VKontakte, and limped along for decades with a loyal but dwindling userbase. In June 2024, the service finally shut down — nearly 28 years after launch. The 'uh oh' sound echoed one last time.
cause_label: Shut down by VK after decades of migration to modern messengers
survived_by: WhatsApp, Telegram, and everyone who still hears the uh-oh sound in dreams.

name: del.icio.us
epitaph: It invented tagging. The web forgot to say thank you.
eulogy: del.icio.us invented social bookmarking and the folksonomy — the idea that ordinary users, not algorithms, could tag and organize the web. It was a treasure chest of the best of the internet, curated by the internet itself. Yahoo acquired it in 2005 for a reported $15-30 million. Yahoo did what Yahoo does. AVOS acquired it in 2011 and quietly drained the life from it. By 2017 the domain was sold to Pinboard's owner, who redirected it, and the original del.icio.us was gone. Its tags still float around the internet like untethered footnotes.
cause_label: Acquired by Yahoo, neglected, and eventually redirected to Pinboard
survived_by: Pinboard, Pocket, and Raindrop.io — and the tags, which live on.

name: AOL Instant Messenger (AIM)
epitaph: Your away message was your first bio.
eulogy: AIM was the social network before social networks. Your away message was your personal brand. The buddy list was your social graph. The door sound — the wooden knock of someone arriving, the creek of someone leaving — was the sound of the 2000s. AOL botched the transition to mobile. iMessage arrived. WhatsApp scaled globally. AIM's userbase evaporated. On December 15, 2017, Oath Inc. (the corporate entity AOL had become) shut it down for good. A generation's first digital relationships ended without fanfare. No takeover offer. No rescue. Just a quiet goodbye page.
survived_by: Every chat app that followed, and the away message — reincarnated as the Instagram bio.

name: Google+
epitaph: Forced upon millions. Loved by dozens.
eulogy: Google+ was created to beat Facebook and became the thing everyone was forced to join to leave a YouTube comment. Google integrated it into every product it owned, boosting signup numbers while the daily active users remained stubbornly low. Then, in 2018, a security bug exposed data from 500,000 users — and Google decided not to disclose it publicly. When that decision became public, the shutdown was announced within weeks. Google+ closed to consumers in April 2019. It had Google Circles, which was genuinely good. That's the kindest thing that can truthfully be said.
cause_label: Shut down by Google following low engagement and API bug
survived_by: Nobody. Not even YouTube comment sections fully recovered.

name: Microsoft Zune
eulogy: The Zune was Microsoft's answer to the iPod, four years too late and one color scheme too strange. It launched in 2006 in a shade of brown that the marketing team called 'cappuccino' and the rest of the world called 'brown.' And yet — the Zune was genuinely good. The interface was elegant. The wireless sync was ahead of its time. The subscription service, Zune Pass, predicted Spotify. Microsoft discontinued hardware in 2011, killed the Zune Marketplace in 2015, and locked owners out of their subscription libraries. Good products die too.
cause_label: Discontinued and shut down by Microsoft
survived_by: Xbox Music → Groove Music → Microsoft's exit from music entirely.

name: Pebble
epitaph: The smartwatch that started it all, with seven days of battery.
eulogy: Pebble made crowdfunding history in 2012, raising over $10 million on Kickstarter for an e-paper smartwatch that lasted a week on a single charge. It created the modern smartwatch category before Apple or Google had even announced a wearable. Developers built thousands of watchfaces and timeline apps for its open SDK. But fierce competition from Apple and Fitbit squeezed its margins. In December 2016, Fitbit acquired Pebble's software assets and abruptly halted hardware production, shutting down its servers. The Pebble community rallied to build Rebble, keeping the beloved watches ticking long after their maker was buried.
cause_label: Acquired by Fitbit and assets/services shut down
survived_by: Rebble, Fitbit OS, and a dedicated community of watch enthusiasts who refuse to take them off.
